title: Earthquakes and Seismic Waves

standard_text: Earthquakes: faults and stress, seismic waves (P, S and surface waves), locating earthquakes, magnitude scales, Earth's layered structure from seismic data, and earthquake hazards in BC. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Geology 12)
meta_desc: Free Geology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): seismic waves, locating earthquakes and magnitude. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: P waves arrive first; S waves cannot travel through liquid.
key_sub: The S–P time tells the distance to the epicentre.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earthquakes happen when stress builds up and rocks suddenly slip along a fault. P waves are compressional and fastest; S waves are shear waves and cannot pass through liquids, which is how we know the outer core is liquid; surface waves cause the most damage.

The time between the P and S arrivals gives the distance to the epicentre; three stations locate it by triangulation. Each step on the magnitude scale is about 10 times more ground motion and about 32 times more energy. BC's coast faces risk from the Cascadia subduction zone.

Example

Which seismic waves cannot pass through the outer core?

Shear waves

Answer: S waves

Example

How many stations are needed to locate an epicentre?

Triangulation

Answer: three

Common mistakes

  • Thinking magnitude 6 is twice as strong as magnitude 3.
  • Mixing up the focus and the epicentre.
  • Thinking S waves are faster than P waves.

faq.q: What is the S-wave shadow zone?
faq.a: The region on the far side of Earth where no S waves arrive, because the outer core is liquid.

faq.q: How can people prepare for earthquakes?
faq.a: Build to earthquake codes, secure heavy objects and practise Drop, Cover and Hold On.
